hits.title: FPP chi=1/3 campaign, 2026-08-15 fire 8: rerouting FATTENS the per-block conditional fourth moment - the campaign's first positive measurement, pre-registered. THE DESIGN IS THE RESULT. Raw kappa4 cannot discriminate for (L2'): a sum of L iid centred uniforms has kurtosis exactly 3 - (6/5)/L, which CONVERGES to 3 as occupation grows, and (L2') holding also predicts a bounded kurtosis near 3 - null and alternative converge on the same number, so enlarging the blocks makes the experiment WEAKER, not stronger. The fix is PAIRING: each resample yields both Delta (rerouting allowed) and Delta_0 (no-reroute, summed over the ORIGINAL geodesic's edges inside the block) on the SAME weights with the SAME occupation, so Delta_0 is an EXACT empirical null and EXCESS := kappa4(Delta) - kappa4(Delta_0), bootstrapped by resampling PAIRS, cancels the occupation confound by construction. GENERAL FORM: when null and alternative converge on the same summary statistic, do not enlarge the experiment - find a statistic on which they diverge. MEASURED, reps sized from a measured first-pass CI half-width: at N=24, 106134 conditional samples, occupation 6.04, reroute fraction 0.383, kappa4 3.048 vs 2.992, excess +0.0557 with 95% CI [0.0263, 0.0843]; at N=40, 45345 samples, occupation 10.09, reroute 0.605, kappa4 3.106 vs 2.920, excess +0.1855 with CI [0.1290, 0.2403]. Both clear of zero and the excess more than triples. NOT A REVERSAL of the underpowered first pass - the N=40 estimate was +0.137 there with half-width 0.18 against +0.186 here with 0.056. HALF-EXPLAINED and flagged at the claim: the excess grows because kappa4(Delta) rises (+0.058) AND the null FALLS (-0.072), the latter against what the fixed-L formula predicts; the plausible cause is occupation VARIANCE differing by size, unmeasured. WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY: (L2') asks whether kappa4 stays BOUNDED, and kappa4 itself is 3.048 and 3.106 - bounded, near Gaussian, moving six hundredths over the whole range. Two points cannot establish a rate. NEXT: 3-4 more occupation points at matched sample counts plus a direct read of occupation variance per size; if the excess keeps climbing with the null controlled, that is the first real evidence AGAINST (L2'), which would take the 9.5 reduction with it. chi = 1/3 UNMOVED.

hits.title: Talagrand's L1-L2 Variance Inequality (the Engine Behind Sublinear Variance)
hits.body:
Let f : {-1,1}^n -> R with the uniform product measure and let Delta_i f (x) = ( f(x) - f(x^{(i)}) ) / 2, where x^{(i)} flips coordinate i. Then there is a UNIVERSAL constant C with Var(f) <= C sum_{i=1}^n || Delta_i f ||_2^2 / ( 1 + log( || Delta_i f ||_2 / || Delta_i f ||_1 ) ), with the convention that a term is 0 when Delta_i f = 0. The unimproved bound Var(f) <= sum_i ||Delta_i f||_2^2 is the Efron-Stein inequality on the cube; Talagrand's refinement gains a LOGARITHMIC factor for every coordinate whose influence is spread out, that is whose L2 and L1 norms are far apart, and gains nothing for a coordinate whose discrete derivative is essentially an indicator. This is precisely the inequality Benjamini, Kalai and Schramm apply to first-passage percolation with two-valued weights to obtain Var <= C n / log n, and the reason their theorem carries a two-point weight hypothesis is that the L1-L2 comparison must be run on that specific cube structure. The p-biased and Gaussian analogues exist with modified constants; the Gaussian version replaces the log ratio by an entropy term (Falik-Samorodnitsky). [Talagrand (1994), 'On Russo's approximate zero-one law', Ann. Probab. 22; used in Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm (2003)]
uniform product measure on the discrete cube {-1,1}^n
f real-valued and square integrable on the cube
C is a universal constant, in particular independent of n and of f

metadata.proof_text: SKETCH. Expand f in the Fourier-Walsh basis and write Var(f) = sum_{S nonempty} fhat(S)^2 = sum_{S nonempty} (1/|S|) sum_{i in S} fhat(S)^2, so that Var(f) <= sum_i sum_{S containing i} fhat(S)^2 / |S| after grouping. The Fourier expansion of Delta_i f is sum_{S containing i} fhat(S) chi_{S minus i}, so || Delta_i f ||_2^2 = sum_{S containing i} fhat(S)^2 and the target is to gain the factor 1/|S| on average. Split each Delta_i f at Fourier level k and apply the hypercontractive moment comparison || g ||_{1 + eps} bounds for low-degree g: the low-degree part of Delta_i f has its L2 norm controlled by (1 + eps)^{k/2} || Delta_i f ||_{1 + eps}, and interpolating the L^{1+eps} norm between L1 and L2 by Holder converts this into a bound involving the ratio || Delta_i f ||_2 / || Delta_i f ||_1. The high-degree part contributes at most (1/k) || Delta_i f ||_2^2 to the weighted sum, by the 1/|S| weight. Optimising k of order log( ||Delta_i f||_2 / ||Delta_i f||_1 ) balances the two contributions and gives the stated bound with an absolute C. The delicate points are the interpolation exponents and the fact that the optimisation must be done per coordinate; both should be re-read in Talagrand's paper before being reused verbatim.

hits.title: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Semigroup and Mehler's Formula
hits.body: Let gamma be the standard Gaussian measure on R^n. The ORNSTEIN-UHLENBECK SEMIGROUP is defined by MEHLER'S FORMULA P_t f(x) = integral f( e^{-t} x + sqrt(1 - e^{-2t}) y ) gamma(dy) for t >= 0. It is a Markov semigroup: P_0 = identity, P_{s+t} = P_s P_t, P_t 1 = 1, P_t preserves nonnegativity, gamma is INVARIANT (integral P_t f dgamma = integral f dgamma), and P_t is SELF-ADJOINT on L^2(gamma). Its generator is L f = Laplacian f - x . grad f, which satisfies the integration-by-parts identity integral (L u) v dgamma = - integral grad u . grad v dgamma. The Hermite polynomials diagonalise it: L He_alpha = - |alpha| He_alpha and P_t He_alpha = e^{-|alpha| t} He_alpha, so the n-th Wiener chaos is the eigenspace of eigenvalue -n. The COMMUTATION RELATION grad P_t f = e^{-t} P_t grad f follows by differentiating Mehler's formula under the integral. Two facts to keep straight: this is the semigroup for the standard Gaussian, and other normalisations of the generator (for example Laplacian/2 minus x . grad/2) rescale time and change the constants in the associated Poincare and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities. As t -> infinity, P_t f -> integral f dgamma, and the exponential rate of that convergence in L^2 is exactly 1, the spectral gap, which is the Gaussian Poincare inequality. [standard; e.g. Bakry, Gentil and Ledoux, Analysis and Geometry of Markov Diffusion Operators, Section 2.7]

metadata.source_revision: standard-definition-2026-08-22; written by the author, with the semigroup property, the invariance of gamma, the Hermite eigenrelation and the commutation relation each verified by direct computation from Mehler's formula

hits.title: A Gaussian field with two well-separated summits has multiple peaks but neither chaos nor superconcentration
hits.body:
PRIVATE AUTHOR-CHECKED DRAFT, no independent review. Let n be even, Z_1, Z_2 independent standard Gaussians, (g_i) independent N(0, sigma^2) with sigma small, and X_i = Z_1 + g_i for i <= n/2, X_i = Z_2 + g_i for i > n/2. Then (a) with probability tending to one as sigma -> 0 there are two near-maximal indices with correlation R = 0 (multiple peaks in Chatterjee's sense with deficit |Z_1 - Z_2| of order one), (b) Var(max_i X_i) -> Var(max(Z_1, Z_2)) > 0, so the field is not superconcentrated relative to its variance scale, and (c) the argmax half is determined by sign(Z_1 - Z_2) and is unchanged under Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise of size t unless t exceeds a level of order |Z_1 - Z_2|, so the field is not chaotic. Hence any multiple-peaks condition that admits two peaks cannot be equivalent to chaos or superconcentration; this refutes the two-peak reading of Chatterjee's open problem 6 in 'Chaos, concentration, and multiple valleys' and leaves the growing-number version open.
Gaussian field on n points as specified
Chatterjee's definitions of multiple peaks, superconcentration and chaos

metadata.proof_text: (a) The maximisers of the two halves are near Z_1 + max g and Z_2 + max g respectively; the two indices lie in different halves and have covariance 0, so R = 0, while the smaller of the two half-maxima is within |Z_1 - Z_2| + O(sigma sqrt(log n)) of the global maximum. (b) max_i X_i = max(Z_1, Z_2) + O(sigma sqrt(log n)) uniformly, so the variance converges to that of max(Z_1, Z_2), which equals 1 - 1/pi > 0. (c) Under the OU flow X^t = e^{-t} X + sqrt(1 - e^{-2t}) X', the half containing the argmax flips only if the noised difference Z_1^t - Z_2^t changes sign, which requires the noise contribution sqrt(1 - e^{-2t}) (Z_1' - Z_2') to exceed e^{-t}|Z_1 - Z_2|; for fixed Z_1 - Z_2 not 0 this has probability tending to 0 as t -> 0, so the overlap between the maximisers at time 0 and time t tends to 1 as t -> 0 uniformly in n, which is the negation of chaos.

hits.title: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Generator on Hilbert Spaces
hits.body:
The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck generator $L$ on $L^2(\Omega; K)$ is defined by $L := -\delta D$ with domain $\operatorname{dom}(L) = \{F \in \mathbb{D}^{1, 2}(K) : D F \in \operatorname{dom}(\delta)\}$. On the Wiener chaos decomposition $F = \sum_{q=0}^\infty J_q F$, $L$ acts as a diagonal operator: $L F = -\sum_{q=1}^\infty q J_q F$. Its pseudo-inverse $L^{-1}$ is defined on centered functionals $F \in L^2(\Omega; K)$ (where $\mathbb{E}[F] = 0$) by $L^{-1} F := -\sum_{q=1}^\infty \frac{1}{q} J_q F$, so that $L L^{-1} F = F$.
F \in L^2(\Omega; K) is centered

hits.title: Conditioning a possibly singular Gaussian: Y given X = x is Gaussian with mean mu_Y + B^T A^+ (x - mu_X) and covariance C - B^T A^+ B
hits.body:
Let (X, Y) be a jointly Gaussian random vector in R^a x R^b with means mu_X, mu_Y and covariance blocks A = Cov(X), B = Cov(X, Y), C = Cov(Y), so its covariance matrix is M = [[A, B], [B^T, C]], possibly singular; A^+ is the Moore-Penrose inverse, and a value x is compatible when x - mu_X lies in the range of A (the support of X). For every compatible x, the conditional law of Y given X = x is Gaussian with mean mu_Y + B^T A^+ (x - mu_X) and covariance K = C - B^T A^+ B, which is positive semidefinite and does not depend on x; and rank M = rank A + rank K.
(X, Y) is jointly Gaussian
x - mu_X lies in the range of A

metadata.domain: finite-dimensional Gaussian vectors with possibly singular covariance
metadata.proof_text: Let R = Y - mu_Y - B^T A^+ (X - mu_X). (X, R) is jointly Gaussian and Cov(X, R) = B - A A^+ B = 0 because the range of B lies in the range of A (the cross-covariance range inclusion), so R is independent of X. Its covariance is C - 2 B^T A^+ B + B^T A^+ A A^+ B = C - B^T A^+ B, using A^+ A A^+ = A^+. Hence given X = x, Y = mu_Y + B^T A^+ (x - mu_X) + R with R ~ N(0, K) independent of X; compatibility makes this a version of the conditional law on the support of X. Finally M = L diag(A, K) L^T with L = [[I, 0], [B^T A^+, I]] invertible, so rank M = rank A + rank K.

hits.title: The innovation of a second Gaussian observation: independent of Y1, covariance S22 - S21 S11^+ S12, cross-covariance D with the state
hits.body:
Let (X, Y1, Y2) be jointly Gaussian with S11 = Cov(Y1), S12 = Cov(Y1, Y2), S22 = Cov(Y2), C1 = Cov(X, Y1), C2 = Cov(X, Y2), possibly singular, with Moore-Penrose inverses; let m1 and K1 be the conditional mean and covariance of X given Y1 = y1, T = S22 - S12^T S11^+ S12, D = C2 - C1 S11^+ S12, and w = y2 - mu2 - S12^T S11^+ (y1 - mu1) the innovation of the second observation. Then W = Y2 - mu2 - S12^T S11^+ (Y1 - mu1) is Gaussian, independent of Y1, with covariance T, and Cov(X, W) = D, which is also the conditional cross-covariance of X and Y2 given Y1.
(X, Y1, Y2) is jointly Gaussian (possibly singular)

metadata.proof_text: This is singular Gaussian conditioning applied to the pair (Y1, Y2): Cov(Y1, W) = S12 - S11 S11^+ S12 = 0 because the range of S12 lies in the range of S11, so W is independent of Y1, and its covariance is the generalized Schur complement T. Cov(X, W) = C2 - C1 S11^+ S12 = D directly.
